register.level: touchy, self-important schoolroom pedant: the 'person of authority' at the pool's bank who treats a dry history primer as a remedy and any slip as a personal insult
register.summary: Two gears only. When he holds the floor he talks like a lecturing usher (Ahem!, Silence all round, if you please!, I proceed) and reads out textbook history. When crossed he flares into short, shrill, offended exclamations and stalks off. Cats and dogs are an unspeakable subject. Per SUP-002 (amended BIB-0027) he is a photoreal CGI mouse; the words stay those of a prim little gentleman, never a squeaking animal (species vocalisation at most a light tic under normal speech).

examples.text: are you all ready? This is the driest thing I know. Silence all round, if you please!
As if I would talk on such a subject! Our family always hated cats: nasty, low, vulgar things! Don't let me hear the name again!
You insult me by talking such nonsense!

catchphrases.text: I beg your pardon! / Did you speak? (icy politeness that is really a rebuke)
cats (and dogs) as a family-honour taboo
my history / a long and a sad tale

sentence_style.length: bimodal: clipped rebukes of 1-6 words (Ahem! / Did you speak? / I had not!) against long quoted primer passages of 30-40 words; mean 11.9 words (median 7) over 22 spoken lines

patterns.rule: Lecturer's command of the room: calls to order and procedural phrases (Sit down, listen to me, Silence all round, if you please, are you all ready, I proceed).

examples.text: Sit down, all of you, and listen to me! I'll soon make you dry enough!
are you all ready? This is the driest thing I know. Silence all round, if you please!
—I proceed. 'Edwin and Morcar, the earls of Mercia and Northumbria, declared for him…'

patterns.rule: Quotes schoolbook English history (the Norman Conquest) word for word as if it were a treatment; the matter is dry, formal, full of earls, archbishops, crowns and usurpation.

examples.text: 'William the Conqueror, whose cause was favoured by the pope, was soon submitted to by the English…'
'—found it advisable to go with Edgar Atheling to meet William and offer him the crown…'

patterns.rule: Offence taken at once and stated as an exclamation: flat contradiction, accusation of inattention or insult, then withdrawal (You are not attending! / I had not! / You insult me…).

examples.text: I shall do nothing of the sort,

patterns.rule: Pedantic echo: throws the challenger's own word back, then lectures them on its meaning (Found it, … of course you know what 'it' means).

examples.text: of course you know what 'it' means.

patterns.rule: Points of order raised with 'But … must …' when a procedure is being settled.

examples.text: But she must have a prize herself, you know,

preferred_fields: English history primer (William the Conqueror, earls, archbishop, crown)
(recited) law-court words: law, trial, jury, judge, prosecute, condemn — only inside his tale

examples.text: Mine is a long and a sad tale!
Fury said to a mouse… 'Let us both go to law: I will prosecute you.' (recited tale, verse)

address.self: I; 'our family' when honour is at stake; stressed I (As if I would…)
address.to_alice: you, and once the condescending 'my dear' while lecturing (How are you getting on now, my dear?)
address.to_group: all of you / if you please (a master to a class)

examples.text: …How are you getting on now, my dear?
Sit down, all of you, and listen to me!

recitation_repertoire.title: the tale of Fury and the mouse (shaped like a tail in the source)
recitation_repertoire.note: type verse: excluded from the back-test denominator; staged as spoken tale, no narration

forbidden_words.reason: he despises what is 'low, vulgar' (ch002-d0046); his English is prim and bookish, the opposite of Bill's or the Gryphon's dialect

forbidden_words.domain: fond or neutral talk of cats and dogs
forbidden_words.reason: the subject is taboo; he only ever names cats/dogs with loathing (ch002-d0039, d0046, d0052)

drift.change: In the pool: shrill, passionate and trembling; short exclamations and a hostile rhetorical question.
Reaching the bank (from ch002-d0052 on) he recovers his dignity and takes the chair: long, formal, lecturing lines and calls to order.
From the tale onward (ch003-d0043) the pompous lecturer collapses back into offended one-liners and he walks off; he is never heard again (only glimpsed splashing in the sister's reverie, ch012-p69).

backtest_markers.regex: \b(ahem|sit down|listen to me|silence all round|if you please|are you all ready|I proceed|driest thing|dry enough)\b
^(I beg your pardon|did you speak|I thought you did)\b
\b(not attending|what are you thinking of|insult|nonsense|nothing of the sort|we indeed|as if I would|hated|vulgar)\b|\bnot!$

backtest.method: marker-claim back-test (shared yardstick with pb1 and 01-story/dialogue-rewrite): a spoken source line hits when it matches >=1 backtest_markers regex and no forbidden_words regex; verse excluded; full definition runs/p3-dialogue-style-pb2/result.json#backtest_method
